name: Heart rate
how_to_measure:
Sit still for 2 minutes.
Place two fingertips on the inside of your wrist, below the thumb.
Count the beats for 15 seconds, or use Count my pulse.
Multiply the count by 4.
why_it_matters: In microgravity, fluids move toward the head and the heart works differently. Heart rate is often one of the first vitals to change with fatigue, illness or dehydration.

name: Systolic blood pressure
how_to_measure:
Rest seated for 5 minutes.
Put the cuff on your upper arm, level with your heart.
Start the monitor and keep still until it finishes.
Record the top number (systolic).
why_it_matters: Fluid shifts in microgravity change blood pressure, especially when you stand up after flight. Readings far from your usual level need a check before any strenuous activity.

name: Diastolic blood pressure
how_to_measure:
Use the same measurement as the systolic reading.
Find the bottom number on the monitor.
Record the bottom number (diastolic).
why_it_matters: Diastolic pressure shows the pressure between heartbeats. It is read together with the systolic value, not on its own.

name: Blood oxygen (SpO2)
how_to_measure:
Clip the probe on a relaxed, warm fingertip.
Keep still until the reading holds steady for 30 seconds.
Record the number shown.
why_it_matters: Cabin air is controlled, but breathing and blood oxygen can still change in flight. Low oxygen can cause dizziness, breathlessness and confusion.

name: Body temperature
how_to_measure:
Take the digital thermometer from the medical kit.
Place it as the kit instructions say and wait for the beep.
Record the reading to one decimal place.
why_it_matters: Infection and dehydration can raise temperature, and a cold cabin or long rest can lower it. Changes should be checked early, because the crew has limited medical resources.

name: Blood glucose
how_to_measure:
Wash and dry your hands.
Prick the side of a fingertip with the lancet.
Apply a drop of blood to the test strip and read the meter.
why_it_matters: Stress, poor sleep and changes in eating during flight can shift blood sugar. Very high or very low readings need prompt action. In the Inspiration4 crew (4 people, 3-day flight), lab glucose averaged 75 mg/dL before launch and 93 mg/dL the day after landing.

name: Sleep last night
how_to_measure:
Think back over the last 24 hours.
Add up all the time you slept, including naps.
Round to the nearest half hour and record it.
why_it_matters: Light and work schedules in orbit and in transit shift sleep. Poor sleep reduces alertness, slows reactions and lowers mood.

name: Mood
how_to_measure:
Look at the five faces, from very low to very good.
Pick the one that best matches how you feel right now.
There is no wrong answer.
why_it_matters: Confinement, isolation and distance from family can lower mood. Low mood often comes before problems with sleep and performance.

name: Reaction time
how_to_measure:
Start the reaction test on the tablet.
Tap the target as soon as it changes colour.
The test runs five times and keeps the median.
why_it_matters: Radiation and sleep loss can affect the brain and reaction speed. Slower reactions raise the risk of mistakes in tasks that need care.

name: Exercise today
how_to_measure:
Think of today's countermeasure sessions.
Add the minutes of treadmill, cycle and resistance exercise.
Enter the total in minutes.
why_it_matters: Without loading, bone and muscle lose strength in microgravity. Daily exercise is the main countermeasure against that loss.

name: Body mass
how_to_measure:
Measure before food or drink, after using the toilet.
Strap in the body mass device and sit still while it moves you on its spring.
Wait for the device to show your mass, then record it to 0.1 kg.
why_it_matters: Body mass can fall in flight when appetite or food intake drops. Watch the trend over several days, not single readings.

name: Back pain
how_to_measure:
Think about your back pain today.
Compare it with the scale: none, mild, moderate, severe or very severe.
Pick the label that fits and note where the pain is in the notes field.
why_it_matters: The spine lengthens in microgravity and back muscles unload. Back pain can disturb sleep and work, and severe or new pain needs a check.

name: Food eaten today
how_to_measure:
Open the food log for today.
Add up the calories printed on each package you ate.
Include drinks with calories and snacks.
Enter the total in kcal.
why_it_matters: In flight, food can taste blander and appetite often drops, so crew can eat less than they burn. Low intake leads to weight loss and muscle and bone loss. Your lower limit is calculated from your sex, age, height and pre-flight mass using the NASA-STD-3001 EER standard (activity factor 1.25, rounded to 10 kcal).

name: Fluids drunk today
how_to_measure:
Count the drink pouches and cups you finished today.
Use the volume printed on each pouch.
Include water, tea, coffee and juice, not food.
Enter the total in mL.
why_it_matters: Thirst is weaker in microgravity and fluid moves toward the head, so crew often drink less than they need. Too little fluid raises heart rate and the risk of kidney stones. The lower limit is the NASA minimum of 2000 mL drinking water a day.

name: Illness symptoms
how_to_measure:
Check for a sore throat, cough, blocked nose or fever feeling.
Check your skin for rash or cold sores.
Compare all of this with the scale: none, mild, moderate, marked or severe.
Pick the label that fits and list the symptoms in the notes.
why_it_matters: Spaceflight stress and a closed cabin change how the immune system works. Old viruses such as cold sores can wake up, and rashes can appear. A small illness spreads fast in a small crew, so report it early.

name: Stress
how_to_measure:
Think about the last 24 hours.
Ask how tense, worried or overloaded you felt.
Pick the label on the scale that fits best.
There is no wrong answer.
why_it_matters: Months in a small, sealed space with high workload and no way out raise stress. Long stress harms sleep, mood and judgement. It often shows before other problems.

name: Social connection
how_to_measure:
Think about the last 24 hours.
Ask how close you felt to your crew and to people at home.
Pick the label on the scale that fits best.
There is no wrong answer.
why_it_matters: Isolation, confinement and distance from family can leave crew feeling alone, even in a full crew. Feeling cut off often comes before low mood and conflict. Talking early helps.

name: Near vision (eye chart)
how_to_measure:
Set up once: hold a bank card to the screen and match the on-screen rectangle to it.
Hold the screen 40 cm from your eyes with both eyes open and your reading glasses on.
For each letter E, tap the direction it points: the side where the three bars end.
The letters get smaller each line. The test stops when you get fewer than 3 of 5 right.
The result is the smallest line you passed. Lower is better; 0.0 is sharp.
why_it_matters: SANS is the main eye risk of long missions. In a NASA study of about 300 astronauts, around 60% on long flights and 29% on short flights reported worse near or distance vision, and some changes were still there years after landing (Mader et al. 2011). The usual complaint is blurred near vision from a far-sighted shift, so near vision is what is tested. This test is a screening estimate to track change from your own baseline, and the ranges here are assumptions.

name: Amsler grid (distorted squares)
how_to_measure:
Set up once: match a bank card to the rectangle on the screen.
Hold the screen about 28 cm from one eye and cover the other eye with your palm.
Look only at the centre dot.
Tap every square that looks wavy, blurred, dark or missing.
Repeat with the other eye. The result is the total squares marked for both eyes.
why_it_matters: NASA has the Amsler grid on the ISS to check the centre of vision. Long missions can cause SANS: a swollen optic nerve, a flattened back of the eye and choroidal folds. About 15% of astronauts had clinically significant optic disc swelling after long flights, and choroidal folds were seen in over 20% (Lee et al. 2020). Any distortion needs a report to the flight surgeon. The 0 and 5 limits here are assumptions.

name: Balance and dizziness
how_to_measure:
Think about the last 24 hours.
Note any dizziness, nausea, spinning or unsteadiness, especially when you move your head.
Pick the label that fits your worst moment.
Note what set it off in the notes field.
why_it_matters: The inner ear senses gravity. In weightlessness it gets mixed signals, which can cause space motion sickness (dizziness, nausea, unsteadiness), mostly in the first days. Balance can also feel unsteady for a few days after landing. Dizziness that stays or is severe needs a check.

name: Urine colour
how_to_measure:
Look at your urine in a clear container or the bowl, in good light.
Compare it with a urine colour chart, from 1 (very pale) to 8 (brown).
Pick the number that is closest.
If you cannot see it well, skip this check.
why_it_matters: Weightlessness releases calcium from bone, which raises the risk of kidney stones, and drinking too little makes stones more likely. Darker urine is a quick sign of low fluid intake. The limits follow published urine colour charts, not NASA limits. Blood in the urine or pain in the side needs medical advice now.

name: Grip strength
how_to_measure:
Use a handgrip dynamometer (a hand squeeze gauge).
Sit or stand with your arm at your side and the elbow bent a little.
Squeeze as hard as you can for 3 seconds.
Do it twice with your stronger hand and type the better value.
why_it_matters: Muscles that carry no weight lose strength in microgravity unless the crew exercise. Grip strength is a simple check of arm strength. Compare it with your own pre-flight value: a steady fall means the exercise plan needs a look. Your watch limit uses the EWGSOP2 low-strength cut-off by sex (27 kg for men, 16 kg for women). These are cut-offs by sex, not severity levels, so the app has no alert limit for grip.
